html:
Egyptian hieroglyphs were the formal writing system of ancient Egypt, a script of picture signs used from about 3200 BCE for more than three thousand years. The name is Greek for "sacred carvings", because Greeks saw them mostly on temples and tombs.

The signs look like pictures of birds, eyes, reeds and people, but most of them stand for sounds. Some stand for single consonants, some for two or three, and others are added to show what a word means. There were more than a thousand signs, though a few hundred were in common use. Vowels were not written.

  • The earliest examples come from royal tombs at Abydos and from objects like the Narmer Palette, from around the founding of the Egyptian state.
  • For everyday writing on papyrus, scribes used quicker joined-up forms, first hieratic and later demotic.
  • Workers in Sinai borrowed a few signs for the sounds of their own language. This was the start of the alphabet that led to the Phoenician alphabet and, through it, to ours.

As Greek and then Christianity spread in Egypt, knowledge of the script faded. The last known hieroglyphic inscription was carved at the temple of Philae in 394 CE. For fourteen centuries no one could read them.

The key was the Rosetta Stone, a decree of 196 BCE from Ptolemaic Egypt, with the same text in hieroglyphs, demotic and Greek. Using it, Jean-François Champollion announced his decipherment in 1822. Like cuneiform in Mesopotamia, it is one of the two oldest writing systems known.
sum: Egyptian hieroglyphs were the formal writing system of ancient Egypt, a script of picture signs used from about 3200 BCE for more than three thousand years. The name is Greek for "sacred carvings", because Greeks saw them mostly on temples …
